title: More than two roads
hook: Pick from many options and check ranges with elif, and, or, not.

warmup.explain: Two equals signs ask the question. One equals sign stores a value. Mix them up and Python shows a SyntaxError.

warmup.q: `age = input("Age? ")`. What kind of thing is age?
options: Text, even if you type digits
warmup.explain: input() always gives text. Wrap it in int() or float() when you need to do maths or compare numbers.
An if line ends with a colon. The lines that belong to it are pushed in by 4 spaces.

why.heading: Two roads are not enough
why.text: A shift can be a short day, a normal day, overtime or double time. A run can be easy, steady or fast. `if` and `else` give only two roads. Real life has more, so Python has `elif`: short for **else if**.

why.heading: elif: first True wins
why.text:
`if hours > 12:` ... `elif hours > 10:` ... `else:`

Python reads from the top. The first condition that is True runs its lines, and ALL the rest are skipped. So order matters: put the biggest limit first. If 11 hours is checked against `> 10` first, it never reaches a bigger rule.

why.heading: and, or, not
why.text:
Join questions together:

`and`: both must be True
`or`: at least one is True
`not`: flips True to False

`day == "Sat" or day == "Sun"` is True on a weekend. `hour >= 6 and hour < 18` is True only in daylight.

why.heading: Checking a range
why.text:
To ask if something sits between two numbers, use `and`:

`if pace >= 4 and pace <= 5:`

That reads: pace is at least 4 AND at most 5. Two small questions, joined. Each side of an `and` must be a whole question.

why.heading: A classic trap with or
why.text: This looks right but is not: `if day == "Sat" or "Sun":`. Python reads `"Sun"` alone as always True, so the if always runs. Write the full question on BOTH sides: `day == "Sat" or day == "Sun"`.

watch.intro: Tap Run. One shift, four possible labels, and a weekend check. Try hours = 13, then 9, then 5.
explain: 11 is not above 12, so the first road is skipped. It is above 10, so `Overtime` runs and the other roads are skipped.
The last `if` starts a fresh question. It is not part of the chain above, so it runs on its own.
`or` is True here because day is `Sat`.
watch.break_it: Break it on purpose: change `elif hours > 10:` to `else if hours > 10:` and run. You get `SyntaxError: expected ':'`. Python has no `else if`, it has `elif`. Put it back. Bonus: swap the order of the two `elif` blocks and run. No error, but 11 now says `Full day`. A wrong order is a bug Python cannot see.

tasks.title: Add the middle road
tasks.task: It is 22 degrees. The program should show `Warm` but shows `Cold`. Add an `elif` between the if and the else: when temp is above 15, show `Warm`.
hints: The new part goes between the if block and the else line.
elif works like if: a condition, a colon, then a pushed-in print.

tasks.title: Day rate label
tasks.task:
Ask for hours worked. Show `Double time` if above 12, `Overtime` if above 10 (11 or 12), otherwise `Normal day`. Example:

`Hours? 11`
`Overtime`
tasks.starter:
hours = int(input("Hours? "))
if hours > 12:
    print("Double time")
# add the middle road and the else
hints: You need one elif and one else under the if that is already there.
The elif condition is hours > 10. It is only reached when hours is NOT above 12.

tasks.title: Can we film now?
tasks.task: Ask for the hour (0 to 23), then ask if it is raining (`yes` or `no`). Show `Go shoot` only when the hour is 6 or later AND before 18 AND it is not raining. Otherwise show `Wait`.
tasks.starter:
hour = int(input("Hour (0-23)? "))
rain = input("Raining (yes/no)? ")
# add your if and else here
hints: Three questions must all be True, so join them with and.
The three questions: hour >= 6, hour < 18, and rain is not yes (use !=).

recap: `elif` is else if. Python takes the first road that is True and skips the rest.
Order matters: check the biggest limit first.
`and` needs both True. `or` needs one. `not` flips the answer.
To check a range, join two comparisons with `and`.

words.meaning: Else if: another question, asked only if the ones above were False.
True only when both sides are True.
True when at least one side is True.
Flips True to False and False to True.
Asking if a number sits between two limits.
